confirmed.title: Supersession misses alias-equivalent facts unless BOTH facts carry the same subject_entity_id
confirmed.summary: gatherSupersessionCandidates' entity scan (readApprovedFactsBySubjectEntity) matches only on stored subject_entity_id equality and never consults the entity's aliases, so a fact written before its entity existed (permanently unlinked — nothing backfills links) or a direct POST /v2/fact without entity ids escapes supersession entirely, leaving two live contradicting 'current' facts for a functional predicate. This is the same defect class the v2.21.1 fix claims to close ('entity aliases were escaping', 'Marcel = Marcel Schmidt'), and round 1 fixed the identical linked-vs-unlinked bridging for L3 reflection grouping but not for the L2 write path.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Executed repro: (1) ingest 'Marcel works_at Google' (valid_from 2024-03-01) before any entity exists -> fact stored unlinked; (2) createEntity 'Marcel Schmidt' (person, alias 'Marcel'); (3) recordFactWithSupersession 'Marcel Schmidt works_at Anthropic' with subject_entity_id and valid_from 2026-07-01 -> decision ADD, supersededIds []; getFactsValidAt(now) returns BOTH 'Anthropic' and 'Google' as current employers. Mirror direction (old fact linked, new POST /v2/fact uses surface alias 'Marcel' with no entity id) also yields ADD with both live. The deterministic-supersession invariant breaks silently; retrieval and L3 see two contradicting current-employment facts.

confirmed.title: Restating a fact inside a closed validity window resurrects it as open-ended current truth
confirmed.summary: Closed facts (valid_to passed) are excluded from the candidate set, so classifyOnWrite's duplicate/stale steps are blind to them: a historical restatement whose event_date falls INSIDE the closed window is classified ADD and written with valid_to null, making the vault assert as currently true something it explicitly recorded as ended — the write-path comment's claim that 'date-based factValidAt at read time recovers correctness' fails here because there is no newer live fact to outrank the resurrected one.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Executed repro: vault holds 'John works_at Google' valid_from 2020-01-01, valid_to 2024-01-01 (closed, ended on its own terms). A 2021-era document ingested today restates 'John works_at Google' with event_date 2021-06-01 (inside the window — zero new information). gatherSupersessionCandidates excludes the closed fact, classifyOnWrite returns ADD, and a new fact 'John works_at Google [2021-06-01 -> null]' is written. getFactsValidAt(now) then returns 'John works_at Google' as the current state, silently contradicting the recorded end date; the correct outcome by the system's own semantics is NONE/stale with provenance merged into the closed covering fact.

confirmed.title: approve-supersedes endpoint allows oldId === newId, leaving an approved fact superseded by itself
confirmed.summary: POST /v2/fact/:newId/approve-supersedes/:oldId never checks oldId !== newId (the same-subject/predicate 400-guard passes trivially for the same record), so after approveFact the endpoint's explicit invalidateFact stamps the just-approved fact with invalidated_at and superseded_by pointing at ITSELF — the reviewer's explicitly approved fact is silently demoted out of retrieval, and a nonsense self-referential supersession edge lands in the graph and any L7 asset built from it; round 1 added exactly this class of guard (self/cycle refusal) for judgments but facts got none.

Resulting record: status=approved, invalidated_at set, superseded_by === own id. The endpoint returns 200 with plausible-looking { approved, invalidated } output; memory-packet and retrieval treat the fact as superseded/contradicted, so the fact the reviewer just approved never surfaces, with no error anywhere.

confirmed.title: Approval-path duplicate merge mutates the survivor fact with no audit entry

A rejected entity's name AND aliases therefore still drive subjKeyOf resolution of unlinked facts: distinct subjects glued together by a rejected (e.g. LLM-hallucinated, reviewer-rejected) entity's alias list tally as one claim group, satisfying Rule A's >=2-distinct-documents gate with one document per real subject. Without the rejected entity, no belief is created (each subject has 1 source). Additionally the map is first-wins on name collisions, so a rejected doppelganger created before an approved entity permanently captures the shared name and re-splits groups — resurrecting the exact split-groups bug the fix targeted.

confirmed.title: ASCII-only tokenizer in consensus entity anchoring renames unrelated facts onto accented entities (v2.21.1 unicode fix not propagated)
confirmed.summary: consensusMerge's tokensOf splits on /[^a-z0-9]+/ (ASCII-only), the exact bug class fixed in v2.21.1 for evidencePassesGate but left unfixed in the anchoring path. An accented entity name fragments into short ASCII tokens ('Zürich' -> ['z','rich'], 'Genève' -> ['gen','ve']); normalizeRef then falsely anchors any unrelated subject/object whose token sequence contains those fragments consecutively, and the emitted fact's subject/object is silently rewritten to the accented entity (lines 501-502 majority-rescue, 530-531 majority path). This also breaks the evidence-rescue invariant: the gate is checked on the pre-rename surface form (line 497) and the fact is renamed afterward, so a stored fact can carry evidence_verified:true while its own verbatim evidence quote never names its subject. The same ASCII-only tokenizer lives in isSelfReferentialTriple (line 74, used to reject facts at api.ts:379). Secondary effect: accented vs transliterated spellings ('Müller AG' vs 'Mueller AG') tally as separate vote keys, splitting consensus votes.

confirmed.title: morphVariants strips -ing/-ed/-es/-s into 1–2 char stems that flood recall and forge titleBoost, burying the only relevant record

confirmed.title: /v2/erase destroys arbitrary files — absolute/relative path escape + owner guard skipped when target has no `owner` frontmatter
confirmed.summary: The erase route builds the target path with `record_path.startsWith('/') ? record_path : join(vaultRoot, record_path)` (absolute paths honored, no vault-containment check) and only enforces ownership with `if (rec.data.owner && rec.data.owner !== owner)`. When the target file's parsed frontmatter has no `owner` key, `rec.data.owner` is undefined, the guard is skipped, and hardErase overwrites the file with a tombstone.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Reproduced live: as ardin, `POST /v2/erase {"record_path":"<abs path>/victim-no-owner.md","reason":"attack"}` where the target is any file with no `owner:` frontmatter (source code, tsconfig, .env, the audit `log.sqlite`, a v1 memory lacking owner, or another tenant's record whose owner field is empty). Response HTTP 200 `{"erased":true,...}` and the file's original content is destroyed and replaced by an `# ERASED` tombstone. Because absolute and `../`-relative paths are not confined to vaultRoot and the owner check is bypassed for owner-less files, any single authenticated tenant can tombstone arbitrary host files — data-loss / availability, and can wipe the hash-chained audit DB. Contrast: the sibling asset routes (wrap/verify/anchor) share the identical `rec.data.owner &&` guard weakness.
skeptic_notes:
CONFIRMED — not refuted. The code at src/v2/api.ts:1036-1051 exactly matches the claim: (1) target path = `record_path.startsWith("/") ? record_path : join(cfg.vaultRoot, record_path)` — absolute paths honored verbatim and relative `../` paths escape the vault, with NO containment/realpath check; (2) the sole ownership guard `if (rec.data.owner && rec.data.owner !== owner)` short-circuits when the target has no `owner` frontmatter (rec.data.owner === undefined), skipping the check entirely. hardErase (layer4-governance.ts:204-236) then atomicWriteFile()s a tombstone over the original content.

Auth cannot save it: owner is derived from the API key (src/api.ts:78-103; x-owner override is env-gated and production-off), so any legitimately authenticated tenant hits this route, and record_path is an unvalidated z.string() (schemas.ts:137-141).

Live reproduction in /tmp using the real gray-matter parser and the exact api.ts:1048 guard: (a) an absolute path to an owner-less file OUTSIDE the vault → data.owner parsed as undefined → guard skipped → file overwritten with tombstone (erased:true); (b) a `../outside/victim-rel.txt` relative path → join() resolves the traversal outside vaultRoot → overwritten. Both original contents destroyed.

Not backlogged: BACKLOG.md has zero erase/traversal/containment/owner-guard entries. Not a round-1 duplicate: research/2026-07-12-general-review-findings.json contains no erase/record_path/containment finding (round-1 grep matched only unrelated entity-link/judgment-supersession/concurrency findings). Not DESIGN INTENT: the design list does not address erase path handling. The claim's contrast is also correct — sibling asset routes (api.ts:1128/1153/1175/1214) share the identical `startsWith("/")` + `rec.data.owner &&` weakness.

This is a real critical security/data-loss vulnerability: a single authenticated tenant can tombstone arbitrary host files (source, config, .env, v1/owner-less records, and even the hash-chained audit log.sqlite whose binary content readFileSync-as-utf8 does not throw and parses to empty frontmatter → guard skipped). The scenario reproduces exactly as described and none of the refutation grounds apply.

Could NOT refute — confirmed live. Reproduced end-to-end through the real buildApi app: authenticated tenant alice POSTs /v2/erase with record_path = absolute path to a file OUTSIDE the vault that has no owner frontmatter; response is HTTP 200 {"erased":true}, and the victim file's original content is destroyed and overwritten with an `# ERASED` tombstone.

1. No vault containment (src/v2/api.ts:1036-1038): `record_path.startsWith("/") ? record_path : join(vaultRoot, record_path)` honors absolute paths verbatim and never checks that the resolved path stays inside vaultRoot; `../` relative paths also escape via join normalization. hardErase (layer4-governance.ts:204-236) repeats the same pattern and calls atomicWriteFile on the arbitrary path. The eraseBody schema (schemas.ts:137) is z.string() with no path restriction.
2. Owner-guard bypass for owner-less files (src/v2/api.ts:1048): `if (rec.data.owner && rec.data.owner !== owner)` — when the parsed frontmatter has no `owner` key, rec.data.owner is undefined and the whole guard short-circuits, so hardErase proceeds. plausible.title: hardErase/ /v2/erase does not cascade — DSAR erasure leaves derived personal data live and recallable
plausible.summary: hardErase tombstones exactly one file and has no callers that cascade. Erasing an L1 episode does not touch the L2 facts derived from it (data/facts, separate files) nor L3 beliefs citing them, even though those records embody the same personal data (subject/predicate/object). The module is documented as the GDPR/nFADP DSAR erasure path.
plausible.failure_scenario: An operator receives a right-to-erasure request for a subject, finds the source episode, and POSTs /v2/erase for it (erased:true). The episode file becomes a tombstone, but the fact `# Marcel located_in Zurich` derived from it remains a live file in data/facts and is still returned by /v2/recall and shown in the graph. The controller believes the personal data is erased while it persists and keeps being surfaced — an incomplete erasure that violates the very GDPR/nFADP guarantee the layer markets, with no warning or enumeration of orphaned derivatives at erase time.
skeptic_notes: The claim's mechanics are accurate — hardErase (src/v2/layer4-governance.ts:197) tombstones exactly one file and /v2/erase (src/v2/api.ts:1027) has no cascade — but the "silent failure / broken guarantee" framing fails against the actual contract. Per-record semantics are explicitly documented at every surface: the MCP tool is "HARD-erase a record by path" (src/mcp.ts:209), the README API table says "Hard-erase a record (tombstone + audit)", the whitepaper says "hardErase overwrites file content with a tombstone", and the input takes a single record_path. A repo-wide grep for "cascade" finds zero promises of cascading or subject-level erasure in src/, docs/, README, CHANGELOG, or BACKLOG, so the operator belief the scenario depends on ("everything about the subject is now erased") is never induced by the system — the response reports erasure of one record only. The GDPR/nFADP wording markets the primitive (true content destruction vs v1's soft forget flag), verified per-record in tests/v2/professional.test.ts:307-330 in exactly that DSAR framing. A complete DSAR is achievable with existing primitives: hardErase is path-generic (works on fact and cognitive files via the same endpoint), subject-level enumeration exists (walkSiblingFacts facts-by-subject at api.ts:1015, /v2/entity/find/:name, /v2/facts/valid-at, /v2/graph/derived-from/:id, derived_from frontmatter on facts), and recall skips tombstones (layer5-retrieval.ts:239) so erased facts stop being surfaced. Moreover the proposed episode→derivatives cascade is itself the wrong DSAR model: erasure requests are subject-centric, so cascading from one source episode would still leave the subject's data from other episodes live and would wrongly destroy facts corroborated by non-erased sources; subject-wide orchestration is controller workflow the system supports but does not claim to automate. This is a feature-scope/convenience gap (no derivative enumeration or warning at erase time), not wrong behavior, data corruption, silent failure, security, or a broken invariant — the endpoint does exactly what it documents.

Claim verified by executed reproduction; could not refute. (1) hardErase (src/v2/layer4-governance.ts:197-262) tombstones exactly one file; its sole caller POST /v2/erase (src/v2/api.ts:1027-1060) passes one record_path and returns {erased:true} with no derivative warning — grep confirms no cascade logic exists anywhere in src/v2. (2) Scratch-vault repro (temp dir, real code): episode "Marcel Keller lives in Zurich" -> approved fact "Marcel Keller located_in Zurich" (derived_from=[episode]) -> hardErase(episode) succeeds -> fact file remains fully intact on disk with the personal data, and recall("Marcel Zurich") still returns the fact as a live hit while correctly skipping the tombstoned episode. (3) No enumeration path at erase time: walkDerivedFrom(episodeId) returns 0 nodes (the walk follows a record's own derived_from links, i.e. fact->episode only, never episode->facts); buildSupportIndex is an internal ranking count, not an exposed reverse lookup. (4) The module explicitly markets itself as the GDPR Art. 17 / nFADP DSAR path (layer4-governance.ts:167-169, WHITEPAPER.md:274-277, README). (5) Not excused: DESIGN INTENT says nothing about erasure scope; BACKLOG.md has zero hits for erase/erasure/dsar/cascade; round-1 findings archive doesn't cover it; existing erase tests only assert the single-file tombstone. The "per-record endpoint as documented" defense fails because the system auto-derives personal data into L2/L3 and gives the operator neither cascade nor enumeration nor warning — the DSAR erasure is silently incomplete, a real silent-failure/broken-invariant.

plausible.title: observe() merges/strips a document's own YAML frontmatter, losing content and forging provenance
plausible.summary: observe() serializes the episode with matter.stringify(input.content, frontmatter); when input.content begins with a '---' YAML fence, gray-matter parses that fence and merges it into the record frontmatter, permanently dropping that portion from the stored content and injecting attacker/document-controlled fields (notably 'source', which observe sets only conditionally).
plausible.failure_scenario:
POST /v2/observe {kind:'document', content:"---
title: Q3 Financial Plan
status: confidential
---
Revenue target is 5M CHF"} with no source. On disk the record frontmatter becomes id/owner/... PLUS title/status merged in, and findEpisode returns content only "Revenue target is 5M CHF" (127-char input -> 61-char readback) — the document's frontmatter is lost from content, breaking the L1 raw-content invariant. Separately, content "---
source: https://trusted.example/official
---
claim" causes findEpisode to report source="https://trusted.example/official" even though observe() returned source:undefined — forged episode provenance. Reproduced in scratch vaults with no flags; reachable directly via /v2/observe.
skeptic_notes:
NOT REFUTED — claim confirmed by executed reproduction. src/v2/layer1-episodic.ts:72 calls matter.stringify(body, frontmatter) where body is raw input.content; gray-matter (4.0.3, the repo's pinned version) re-parses string input in stringify, so a leading '---' YAML fence in the document is consumed as data and merged into the record frontmatter via Object.assign({}, file.data, data). Scratch-vault run (repro.ts, using the repo's own observe/findEpisode + initAudit): (A) content "---
title: Q3 Financial Plan
status: confidential
---
Revenue target is 5M CHF" (78 chars) stored with title/status injected into record frontmatter and readback content reduced to "Revenue target is 5M CHF" (24 chars) — the document's frontmatter is permanently lost from L1 raw content, and even the filename slug leaked the merged keys; (B) content with its own "source: https://trusted.example/official" fence: observe() returned source undefined, but findEpisode returned that URL as the episode's source — forged provenance, exactly because observe sets source only conditionally (line 56); (C) protected keys (id/owner/actor/kind/timestamp) are NOT forgeable since record data wins the merge, matching the claim's scope. Reachable via /v2/observe (api.ts:303-308) with no content sanitization. Not on DESIGN INTENT, not in BACKLOG.md, absent from the round-1 findings archive and v2210-review-fixes tests. Only the claim's example char counts (127→61) differ cosmetically from measured (78→24); mechanism and both failure modes are exact.

The gray-matter re-parse mechanism reproduces (confirmed in scratch vaults: a document beginning with a '---' YAML fence gets merged into record frontmatter and stripped from findEpisode().content; a doc-injected 'source' field sets episode.source even when observe was called with source:undefined). However, the claim's "[major] losing content and forging provenance" framing is refuted:

1. No content is lost on disk. Repro case 1 shows the document's title/status are preserved in the record frontmatter and the whole document remains a human-readable .md. The only stated L1 invariant ("each episode is a .md file the user can read") holds. There is no invariant that findEpisode().content is byte-identical to input; the frontmatter is relocated to structured metadata, not deleted.

2. The security-critical forgery vectors are impossible. Repro 2 proves id/owner/kind/timestamp/actor CANNOT be overridden by document frontmatter — gray-matter's stringify does Object.assign({}, file.data, data) with observe's real frontmatter applied last, so it wins. No cross-owner injection, no ID collision.

3. The only injectable field is `source`, which is not a trust/verification anchor. Downstream it is used only as a graph label (layer5-graph-view.ts:137) and a slug seed. Fact provenance flows through derived_from=[ep.id], and layer4/UAL hashing uses fact source_content, not episode.source. A markdown document declaring its own source in frontmatter is plausibly-legitimate metadata, consistent with the repo's explicit Obsidian-frontmatter-compatibility design goal. "Forged provenance" overstates a non-security informational field.

4. Fact extraction is unaffected: api.ts passes parsed.body.content (the original full text including the frontmatter) to extractor.extract(), so no facts are lost or corrupted.

This is at most a minor behavioral quirk of storing markdown documents that already carry frontmatter (standard gray-matter behavior aligned with the stated Obsidian-compat design), not data corruption, silent failure, security, or a broken invariant. Refuted.
